claim: HIV-1 generates unspliced (US), partially spliced (PS), and completely spliced (CS) classes of RNAs, each playing distinct roles in viral replication.
source: HIV-1 generates unspliced (US), partially spliced (PS), and completely spliced (CS) classes of RNAs, each playing distinct roles in viral replication.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational claim about HIV-1 RNA biology and is supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: HyPR-MSSV enables isolation of US, PS, and CS transcripts from a single population of infected CD4+ T-cells.
source: Here, we present HyPR-MSSV for isolation of US, PS, and CS transcripts from a single population of infected CD4+ T-cells and mass spectrometric identification of their in vivo protein interactomes.
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes the development and capability of the HyPR-MSSV method.

claim: 212 proteins were identified as differentially associated with the unique HIV-1 RNA classes.
source: Analysis revealed 212 proteins differentially associated with the unique RNA classes, including preferential association of regulators of RNA stability with US and PS transcripts and, unexpectedly, mitochondria-linked proteins with US transcripts.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the mass spectrometry analysis reported in the abstract.

claim: Regulators of RNA stability preferentially associate with US and PS transcripts.
source: Analysis revealed 212 proteins differentially associated with the unique RNA classes, including preferential association of regulators of RNA stability with US and PS transcripts and, unexpectedly, mitochondria-linked proteins with US transcripts.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract as a finding from the analysis.

claim: Mitochondria-linked proteins preferentially associate with US transcripts.
source: Analysis revealed 212 proteins differentially associated with the unique RNA classes, including preferential association of regulators of RNA stability with US and PS transcripts and, unexpectedly, mitochondria-linked proteins with US transcripts.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract as an unexpected finding.

claim: More than 80 of the identified factors impacted HIV-1 gene expression when knocked down by siRNA.
source: Remarkably, >80 of these factors screened by siRNA knockdown impacted HIV-1 gene expression.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a result from the siRNA knockdown screen.

claim: Several identified host proteins co-localize with HIV-1 US RNA.
source: Fluorescence microscopy confirmed several to co-localize with HIV-1 US RNA and exhibit changes in abundance and/or localization over the course of infection.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from fluorescence microscopy experiments.

claim: Several identified host proteins exhibit changes in abundance and/or localization over the course of HIV-1 infection.
source: Fluorescence microscopy confirmed several to co-localize with HIV-1 US RNA and exhibit changes in abundance and/or localization over the course of infection.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from fluorescence microscopy experiments.

claim: HIV-1 uses alternative splicing of a single primary RNA transcript to produce three major classes of viral RNA variants: unspliced (US), partially spliced (PS), and completely spliced (CS).
source: HIV-1 uses the alternative splicing of a single primary RNA transcript to produce three major classes of viral RNA variants: unspliced (US), partially spliced (PS), and completely spliced (CS).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and is established knowledge in HIV-1 biology.

claim: Individual HIV-1 splice variants perform distinct roles during HIV-1 replication through dynamic interactions with specific viral and host proteins.
source: The individual variants perform distinct roles during HIV-1 replication through dynamic interactions with specific viral and host proteins (Coffin et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Each HIV-1 splice variant is predicted to interface with a unique protein interactome.
source: Each HIV-1 splice variant performs a distinct function and is thus predicted to interface with a unique protein interactome.
evidence: This is a prediction stated in the Introduction based on the distinct functions of splice variants.

claim: Early HIV-1 gene expression involves translation of auxiliary proteins Tat and Rev as well as the accessory protein Nef from CS transcripts.
source: Early gene expression involves translation of auxiliary proteins Tat and Rev as well as the accessory protein Nef from CS transcripts.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as established knowledge about HIV-1 gene expression.

claim: Tat and Rev localize to the nucleus where Tat facilitates viral transcription and Rev mediates nuclear export of intron-retaining US and PS transcripts.
source: Tat and Rev localize to the nucleus where Tat facilitates viral transcription and Rev mediates nuclear export of intron-retaining US and PS transcripts.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as established knowledge about HIV-1 gene expression.

claim: Late HIV-1 gene expression is marked by translation of the US transcript to synthesize Gag and Gag-Pol capsid proteins.
source: Late gene expression is marked by translation of the US transcript to synthesize Gag and Gag-Pol capsid proteins and translation of PS transcripts to generate Envelope glycoproteins as well as the Vpu, Vpr, and Vif immunomodulatory factors.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as established knowledge about HIV-1 gene expression.

claim: Late HIV-1 gene expression includes translation of PS transcripts to generate Envelope glycoproteins as well as the Vpu, Vpr, and Vif immunomodulatory factors.
source: Late gene expression is marked by translation of the US transcript to synthesize Gag and Gag-Pol capsid proteins and translation of PS transcripts to generate Envelope glycoproteins as well as the Vpu, Vpr, and Vif immunomodulatory factors.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as established knowledge about HIV-1 gene expression.

claim: HIV-1 splicing generates over 50 splice variants proposed to be physiologically significant.
source: HIV-1 splicing generates vast numbers of splice variants, with over 50 proposed to be physiologically significant (Emery et al., 2017; Ocwieja et al., 2012; Purcell and Martin, 1993; Vega et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: HIV-1 US and PS transcripts hijack the cellular XPO1 (also known as CRM1)-mediated nuclear export pathway through the activities of Rev and the Rev-response element (RRE).
source: For example, HIV-1 US and PS transcripts hijack the cellular XPO1 (also known as CRM1)-mediated nuclear export pathway through the activities of Rev and a cis-acting RNA structure known as the Rev-response element (RRE) (Pollard and Malim, 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Rev multimerizes on the RRE and recruits XPO1 to form a functional RNA export complex.
source: Rev multimerizes on the RRE and recruits XPO1 to form a functional RNA export complex (Bai et al., 2014; Daugherty et al., 2008; Daugherty et al., 2010; DiMattia et al., 2016; DiMattia et al., 2010; Fang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: CS transcripts do not require Rev and recruit components of the NXF1/NXT1 export machinery, similar to the bulk of cellular fully spliced mRNAs.
source: This is in contrast to CS transcripts that do not require Rev and recruit components of the NXF1/NXT1 export machinery, similar to the bulk of cellular fully spliced mRNAs.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as established knowledge about CS transcript export.

claim: US HIV-1 transcripts are packaged into virions due to favored interactions between the Gag polyprotein and a structured RNA packaging signal known as 'psi' in the 5'-untranslated region of the US transcript.
source: A second example is HIV-1 genome packaging wherein US transcripts are packaged into virions due to favored interactions between the Gag polyprotein and a structured RNA packaging signal known as 'psi' in the 5'-untranslated region of the US transcript (Berkowitz et al., 1993; Lever et al., 1989; Luban and Goff, 1994).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: The psi packaging signal binding sites are lost in PS and CS transcripts due to splicing.
source: These binding sites are lost in PS and CS transcripts due to splicing (Purcell and Martin, 1993).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Over 200 proteins were identified as differentially associated with the US, PS, and CS HIV splice variant pools.
source: We identify over 200 proteins differentially associated with the US, PS, and CS HIV splice variant pools, 102 of which are previously unkown HIV-1-host interactors.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as a primary finding of the study.

claim: 102 of the identified differentially associated proteins are previously unknown HIV-1-host interactors.
source: We identify over 200 proteins differentially associated with the US, PS, and CS HIV splice variant pools, 102 of which are previously unkown HIV-1-host interactors.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as a primary finding of the study.

claim: Gene-specific siRNA knockdown of 121 host proteins indicated more than 80 are effectors of HIV-1 RNA regulation.
source: Gene-specific siRNA knockdown (KD) of 121 host proteins indicated more than 80 are effectors of HIV-1 RNA regulation.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as a finding from the siRNA screen.

claim: Three biotinylated capture oligonucleotides were designed complementary to three distinct regions of the HIV RNA genome: intron-1 (unique to US), intron-2 (present in both US and PS), and the 3'-exon (present in US, PS, and CS).
source: To isolate the US, PS, and CS RNA pools, three biotinylated capture oligonucleotides (COs) were designed complementary to three distinct regions of the HIV RNA genome: intron-1 (unique to US), intron-2 (present in both US and PS), and the 3'-exon (present in US, PS, and CS) (Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Jurkat cultures were treated with formaldehyde at 48 hr post-infection to preserve in vivo viral RNA-protein complexes prior to cell lysis.
source: To preserve in vivo viral RNA-protein complexes prior to cell lysis, Jurkat cultures were treated with formaldehyde at 48 hr post-infection (h.p.i.) (multiplicity of infection [MOI] of ~1 infectious unit per cell).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as part of the experimental procedure.

claim: The Jurkat cell line was chosen because it is a well-characterized CD4+ T-cell line previously confirmed to support replication of the HIV-1NL4-3 reporter virus.
source: The Jurkat cell line was chosen because it is a well-characterized CD4+ T-cell line previously confirmed to support replication of the HIV-1NL4-3 reporter virus used for this study (Knoener et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: Enrichment of each HIV transcript over a cellular control transcript (GAPDH) was >100-fold.
source: Enrichment of each HIV transcript over a cellular control transcript (GAPDH) was >100-fold (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Capture efficiency was >70% for each HIV-1 splice variant.
source: Capture efficiency (the amount of each transcript depleted from the lysate after capture) was >70% for each variant (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 926 proteins were identified in at least two biological replicates of all three HIV splice variant captures.
source: In all, 926 proteins were identified in at least two biological replicates of all three HIV splice variant captures (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: More than two-thirds (633) of the common interactors were previously identified in at least one prior study identifying proteins associated with cellular polyadenylated mRNA.
source: More than two-thirds (633) of these common interactors were previously identified in at least one prior study identifying proteins associated with cellular polyadenylated mRNA (Hentze et al., 2018; Queiroz et al., 2019; Supplementary file 2), and thus likely represent RNA-associated proteins with general roles in mRNA processing, transport, and translation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: Common interactors include host factors regulating RNA transport and translational initiation (e.g., NCBP1, DHX9, DDX3, EIF4G, and PABP).
source: These common interactors also featured several proteins previously implicated in HIV-1 replication including host factors regulating RNA transport and translational initation (e.g., NCBP1, DHX9, DDX3, EIF4G, and PABP) (Boeras et al., 2016; Bolinger et al., 2010; Soto-Rifo et al., 2013; Stake et al., 2015; Yedavalli et al., 2004)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Common interactors include known HIV splicing factors (e.g., HMGA1, HNRNPA1, HNRNPAB, HNRNPH, HNRNPF, SRSF1, SRSF2, SRSF3, SRSF6, SRSF7, TRA2B, and U2AF2).
source: known HIV splicing factors (e.g., HMGA1, HNRNPA1, HNRNPAB, HNRNPH, HNRNPF, SRSF1, SRSF2, SRSF3, SRSF6, SRSF7, TRA2B, and U2AF2) (Dlamini and Hull, 2017; Mahiet and Swanson, 2016; Sertznig et al., 2018; Stoltzfus and Madsen, 2006)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Using the Student's t-test and a permutation-based false discovery rate (FDR) of 5%, 212 proteins were identified that differentially interacted with one or more of the HIV splice variant classes: 101, 93, and 68 proteins in the US, PS, and CS captures, respectively.
source: Using the Student's t-test and a permutation-based false discovery rate (FDR) of 5%, we identified 212 proteins that differentially interacted with one or more of the HIV splice variant classes: 101, 93, and 68 proteins in the US, PS, and CS captures, respectively (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from statistical analysis of mass spectrometry data.

claim: 45 proteins were preferentially associated with both the US and PS HIV transcripts but not the CS pool.
source: The most abundant of these were proteins preferentially associated with both the US and PS HIV transcripts but not the CS pool (45 proteins) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Nine proteins known to regulate RNA stability were associated with both the US and PS, but not CS, transcripts (FXR1, YBX1, YBX3, IGF2BP1, IGF2BP3, SYNCRIP, HNRNPR, YTHDF2, and UPF1).
source: Notable among these were nine proteins, known to regulate RNA stability, associated with both the US and PS, but not CS, transcripts (FXR1, YBX1, YBX3, IGF2BP1, IGF2BP3, SYNCRIP, HNRNPR, YTHDF2, and UPF1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from GO term enrichment analysis.

claim: Proteins involved in mRNA splicing and its regulation were elevated in the US and PS relative to the CS capture samples (YBX1, SYNCRIP, HNRNPR, HNRNPL, BCAS2, RBMX, and MBNL1).
source: Proteins involved in mRNA splicing, and the regulation thereof, were also elevated in the US and PS relative to the CS capture samples (YBX1, SYNCRIP, HNRNPR, HNRNPL, BCAS2, RBMX, and MBNL1) but with less congruence.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from GO term enrichment analysis.

claim: HNRNPA2B1 and HNRNPK (negative regulators of splicing) were elevated only in the US capture samples.
source: A subset of these proteins were elevated only in the US capture samples (HNRNPA2B1 and HNRNPK; negative regulators of splicing) or PS capture samples (DAZAP1 and TRA2A; positive regulators of splicing), but not in both.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from GO term enrichment analysis.

claim: DAZAP1 and TRA2A (positive regulators of splicing) were elevated only in PS capture samples.
source: A subset of these proteins were elevated only in the US capture samples (HNRNPA2B1 and HNRNPK; negative regulators of splicing) or PS capture samples (DAZAP1 and TRA2A; positive regulators of splicing), but not in both.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from GO term enrichment analysis.

claim: PS captures were exclusively enriched for proteins found in nuclear bodies.
source: PS captures were also exclusively enriched for proteins found in nuclear bodies.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from GO term enrichment analysis.

claim: Proteins involved in translation were highly enriched in both the US (12 proteins) and CS (18 proteins) interactomes.
source: For cytoplasmic activities, proteins involved in translation were highly enriched in both the US (12 proteins) and CS (18 proteins) interactomes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from GO term enrichment analysis.

claim: The CS interactome included translation initiation proteins.
source: Interestingly, however, while the CS interactome included translation initiation proteins (as may be expected), the US interactome was enriched for proteins linked to mRNA translation in the mitochondria.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from GO term enrichment analysis.

claim: The US interactome was enriched for proteins linked to mRNA translation in the mitochondria.
source: Interestingly, however, while the CS interactome included translation initiation proteins (as may be expected), the US interactome was enriched for proteins linked to mRNA translation in the mitochondria.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from GO term enrichment analysis.

claim: 45 mitochondrion proteins were enriched in the US RNA interactome.
source: Cellular component GO term enrichment analysis further revealed 45 mitochondrion proteins enriched in the US RNA interactome; eight are mitochondrial nucleoid proteins and several have known roles in the carboxylic acid metabolic process, a GO term also over-represented in the US RNA interactome (Figure 2C, Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Eight of the mitochondrion proteins enriched in the US RNA interactome are mitochondrial nucleoid proteins.
source: Cellular component GO term enrichment analysis further revealed 45 mitochondrion proteins enriched in the US RNA interactome; eight are mitochondrial nucleoid proteins and several have known roles in the carboxylic acid metabolic process, a GO term also over-represented in the US RNA interactome (Figure 2C, Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 121 host proteins identified by HyPR-MSSV were targeted for siRNA knockdown and passed cell viability criteria in HEK293T cells.
source: To determine their potential relevance to HIV-1 gene expression, 121 host proteins identified by HyPR-MSSV were targeted for siRNA KD (Supplementary file 3) and passed cell viability criteria in HEK293T cells (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as part of the validation experiments.

claim: Statistically significant changes (p-value<0.05) to early (CS) and/or late (US) gene expression were observed for 69% (84 of 121) of the targeted host genes.
source: Relative to a scrambled siRNA control, statistically significant changes (p-value<0.05) to early (CS) and/or late (US) gene expression were observed for a remarkable 69% (84 of 121) of the targeted host genes (Figure 3C; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The knockdown of 33 host proteins affected the expression of US and CS protein products in the same direction and with approximately the same magnitude.
source: The KD of 33 host proteins affected the expression of US and CS protein products in the same direction (either both increased or both decreased) and with approximately the same magnitude.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from the siRNA screen.

claim: CS and US protein expression were differentially affected by knockdown of 51 host proteins.
source: By comparing mCherry:CFP fluorescence ratios for each protein KD to the negative control, we determined that CS and US protein expression were differentially affected by KD of 51 host proteins; for 26 of the proteins the expression changes were in the same direction but with different magnitudes; for 18 only the expression of the US RNA protein product was affected; and for seven only the expression of the CS RNA protein product was affected (Figure 3C, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: 71 host genes were categorized as putative 'positive' effectors and 16 as putative 'negative' effectors based on the direction of changes in HIV-1 gene expression.
source: Based on the direction of the changes in HIV-1 gene expression (increased or decreased), we categorized 71 host genes as putative 'positive' effectors and 16 as putative 'negative' effectors (Figure 3C, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Of the 16 negative effectors, 10 were implicated in mitochondria-associated pathways based on GO analysis.
source: Interestingly, of the 16 negative effectors, 10 were implicated in mitochondria-associated pathways based on GO analysis; of those ten, nine were identified by HyPR-MSsv to preferentially interact with the US HIV RNA (Figure 2—source data 2, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from the siRNA screen and GO analysis.

claim: Of the 10 negative effectors implicated in mitochondria-associated pathways, nine were identified by HyPR-MSSV to preferentially interact with the US HIV RNA.
source: Interestingly, of the 16 negative effectors, 10 were implicated in mitochondria-associated pathways based on GO analysis; of those ten, nine were identified by HyPR-MSsv to preferentially interact with the US HIV RNA (Figure 2—source data 2, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from the siRNA screen and HyPR-MSSV analysis.

claim: Seventeen of the 18 host proteins were detected by immunofluorescence and showed >40% decreases in IF signal after host protein siRNA knockdown.
source: Seventeen of the 18 host proteins (all but DLD) were detected by IF and showed >40% decreases in IF signal after host protein siRNA KD.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from immunofluorescence validation.

claim: Imaging-based analysis allowed verification of the efficacy of siRNA knockdown for three host proteins (IGF2BP3, SRRM2, and DNM2) that could not be detected using immunoblot.
source: This imaging-based analysis also allowed verification of the efficacy of siRNA KD for three of the host proteins (IGF2BP3, SRRM2, and DNM2) that we had been unable to detect using immunoblot (Supplementary file 8).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from immunofluorescence validation.

claim: Consistent co-localization of US HIV-1 RNA with 11 host proteins was observed by single-cell fluorescence microscopy.
source: Analysis by single-cell fluorescence microscopy showed consistent co-localization of US HIV-1 RNA with 11 of the proteins (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplements 1–3)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A and supplementary figures.

claim: Four host proteins (HNRNPR, RBMX, RBM4, MBOAT7) were predominantly localized to the nucleus or near the nuclear membrane in uninfected cells.
source: with four (HNRNPR, RBMX, RBM4, MBOAT7) predominantly localized to the nucleus or near the nuclear membrane and seven (FAM120A, IGF2BP3, MOV10, TRIM56, DNM2, LRPPRC, CSDE1) predominantly localized to the cytoplasm in uninfected cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Seven host proteins (FAM120A, IGF2BP3, MOV10, TRIM56, DNM2, LRPPRC, CSDE1) were predominantly localized to the cytoplasm in uninfected cells.
source: with four (HNRNPR, RBMX, RBM4, MBOAT7) predominantly localized to the nucleus or near the nuclear membrane and seven (FAM120A, IGF2BP3, MOV10, TRIM56, DNM2, LRPPRC, CSDE1) predominantly localized to the cytoplasm in uninfected cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Five recurrent US RNA-host protein co-localization phenotypes were observed: at nuclear puncta, at puncta proximal to the nuclear membrane, at cytoplasmic puncta, at large cytoplasmic complexes reminiscent of stress granules, and at the plasma membrane.
source: In infected cells, we observed five recurrent US RNA-host protein co-localization phenotypes: (1) at nuclear puncta, (2) at puncta proximal to the nuclear membrane, (3) at cytoplasmic puncta, (4) at large, cytoplasmic complexes reminiscent of stress granules, and (5) at the plasma membrane (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A and supplementary figures.

claim: One or two bright US RNA puncta per cell were typically observed in the nucleus, consistent with prior reports describing sites of active HIV-1 transcription.
source: In the nucleus, we typically observed one or two bright US RNA puncta per cell, consistent with prior reports describing sites of active HIV-1 transcription (Puray-Chavez et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: Proteins that predominantly localize to the nucleus or proximal to the nuclear membrane (HNRNPR, RBMX, RBM4, MBOAT7) had a higher frequency of co-localization with HIV RNA at nuclear puncta (57–96%) relative to proteins predominantly localized to the cytoplasm (FAM120A, IGF2BP3, MOV10, DNM2, TRIM56, LRPPRC, CSDE1; 0–8%).
source: The data revealed that proteins that predominantly localize to the nucleus or proximal to the nuclear membrane (HNRNPR, RBMX, RBM4, MBOAT7) had a higher frequency of co-localization with HIV RNA at nuclear puncta (57–96%) relative to proteins that were predominantly localized to the cytoplasm (FAM120A, IGF2BP3, MOV10, DNM2, TRIM56, LRPPRC, CSDE1; 0–8%).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from quantification of co-localization phenotypes.

claim: HNRNPR and RBMX co-localized frequently with HIV-1 US RNA at all four quantified sites (41–90%).
source: Two proteins (HNRNPR and RBMX) co-localized frequently with HIV-1 US RNA at all four quantified sites (41–90%).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from quantification of co-localization phenotypes.

claim: All 11 host proteins co-localized with US RNA at small cytoplasmic puncta in a high percentage of cells (71–100%).
source: All 11 host proteins co-localized with US RNA at small cytoplasmic puncta in a high percentage of cells (71–100%) with most (all but LRPPRC and MBOAT7) co-localizing with US RNA at the plasma membrane (31–100% of cells), generally with Gag also present (Figure 4B, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Most host proteins (all but LRPPRC and MBOAT7) co-localized with US RNA at the plasma membrane (31–100% of cells), generally with Gag also present.
source: All 11 host proteins co-localized with US RNA at small cytoplasmic puncta in a high percentage of cells (71–100%) with most (all but LRPPRC and MBOAT7) co-localizing with US RNA at the plasma membrane (31–100% of cells), generally with Gag also present (Figure 4B, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: HNRNPR, FAM120A, and IGF2BP3 exhibited four US HIV RNA co-localization phenotypes (nuclear puncta, cytoplasmic granules, cytoplasmic puncta, and plasma membrane puncta).
source: Of these, HNRNPR, FAM120A, and IGF2BP3 were of particular interest because all three exhibited four US HIV RNA co-localization phenotypes (nuclear puncta, cytoplasmic granules, cytoplasmic puncta, and plasma membrane puncta) (Figure 4B)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: HNRNPR, FAM120A, and IGF2BP3 preferentially interacted with US and PS, but not CS, HIV RNA as determined by HyPR-MSSV.
source: preferentially interacted with US and PS, but not CS, HIV RNA as determined by HyPR-MSSV (Figure 4C, Supplementary file 4)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: HNRNPR, FAM120A, and IGF2BP3 showed similar trends in gene expression upon siRNA knockdown (both US and CS expression decreased, with a marginally greater decrease in US expression).
source: and showed similar trends in gene expression upon siRNA KD (both US and CS expression decreased, with a marginally greater decrease in US expression) (Figure 4D, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: LRPPRC localizes to the mitochondria as well as the nucleus.
source: By contrast, LRPPRC, a protein shown to localize to the mitochondria as well as the nucleus (Mili and Piñol-Roma, 2003; Ruzzenente et al., 2012)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: MBOAT7 localizes to mitochondria-associated membranes.
source: and MBOAT7, a protein shown to localize to mitochondria-associated membranes (Hirata et al., 2013)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: LRPPRC and MBOAT7 localized to US HIV RNA nuclear puncta, at perinuclear puncta, and at cytoplasmic puncta but were not observed to co-localize with US RNA and Gag at the plasma membrane.
source: localized to US HIV RNA nuclear puncta, at perinuclear puncta, and at cytoplasmic puncta but were not observed to co-localize with US RNA and Gag at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from co-localization analysis.

claim: LRPPRC and MBOAT7 were preferentially associated with US and PS, relative to CS, transcripts based on HyPR-MSSV analysis.
source: Similar to HNRNPR/FAM120A/IGF2BP3, both LRPPRC and MBOAT7 were preferentially associated with US and PS, relative to CS, transcripts based on HyPR-MSSV analysis.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a finding from HyPR-MSSV analysis.

claim: LRPPRC and MBOAT7 were negative effectors of both US and CS HIV-1 gene expression.
source: However, unlike HNRNPR/FAM120A/IGF2BP3, each of these proteins were negative effectors of both US and CS HIV-1 gene expression (Figure 4D, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: LRPPRC was detected not only near transcription sites but also in a trail-like pattern that extended to the periphery of the nucleus.
source: Interestingly, LRPPRC was detected not only near transcription sites but also in a trail-like pattern that extended to the periphery of the nucleus (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplements 1–3)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A and supplementary figures.

claim: MBOAT7 was observed at transcription sites, at smaller subnuclear US HIV RNA puncta, and with high frequency and abundance at US RNA puncta at or near the nuclear membrane.
source: and MBOAT7 was observed at transcription sites, at smaller subnuclear US HIV RNA puncta, and with high frequency and abundance at US RNA puncta at or near the nuclear membrane (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A and supplementary figures.

claim: HNRNPR was primarily localized to the nucleus of cells expressing no, or low amounts of, Gag and US RNA, but exhibited marked shifts from the nucleus to the cytoplasm in cells with high levels of Gag and US RNA expression.
source: For example, HNRNPR, generally a nuclear protein, was primarily localized to the nucleus of cells expressing no, or low amounts of, Gag and US RNA, but exhibited marked shifts from the nucleus to the cytoplasm in cells with high levels of Gag and US RNA expression (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: MBOAT7 showed much higher levels of expression in cells with abundant Gag and US RNA than in uninfected or early infected cells.
source: Changes to MBOAT7 were also striking, with much higher levels of expression in cells with abundant Gag and US RNA than in uninfected or early infected cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Each of the 12 host proteins exhibited non-random, bimodal expression changes from 'early' and 'late' HIV gene expression.
source: In general, each host protein exhibited non-random, bimodal expression changes from 'early' and 'late' HIV gene expression (Figure 5—figure supplements 1–4, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5 supplementary figures.

claim: In early/uninfected cells, linear increases in HNRNPR and MBOAT7 expression were observed, positively correlating with subtle increases in US HIV RNA expression.
